title: Placaeus: the power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning
source_text: XXIV. Sic etiam ea de re pronunciat Josue Placeus thesi jam allegata. Tam naturalis, inquit, erat Adamo facultas non moriendi, quam non peccandi. Haud magis est a natura mortis quam peccati imperium. Possibilitatem quidem moriendi a natura habuit, necessitatem vero a peccato. Cujus rei hanc rationem affert, quod aequum sit facultates Physicas sequi conditionem Moralium, penes quas est imperium in homine: Unde colligit in Adamo eandem fuisse rationem vitae & justitiae. Ac proinde cum justitia ipsi fuerit naturalis, naturalem quoque esse debuisse non moriendi facultatem.
pass_a_gloss: So also Josué de la Place pronounces on the matter in the thesis already cited. As natural, he says, was to Adam the faculty of not dying, as of not sinning. Not more is the dominion of death from nature than that of sin. The possibility indeed of dying he had from nature, but the necessity from sin. For which matter he brings this reason, that it is fair that the Physical faculties follow the condition of the Moral, with which lies the rule in man: Whence he gathers that in Adam the account of life and of justice was the same. And therefore since justice was natural to him, the faculty of not dying also ought to have been natural.
pass_b_english: Josué de la Place says the same in the thesis already cited: "The power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning. The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin. He had the possibility of dying from nature, but the necessity of dying from sin."

He gives this reason: it is fitting that the physical powers follow the condition of the moral powers, which rule in man. From this he concludes that in Adam life and righteousness stood on the same footing, and so, since righteousness was natural to him, the power of not dying must have been natural too.

choices.english: The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin
